> [!TIP]
> Start with `potential: false` to generate an unguided ensemble, then measure its $R_g$ distribution and PRE violations. Use the observed deviation to calibrate `timescale`—if the unguided ensemble already partially satisfies restraints, a lower `timescale` (3–5) suffices. If violations are severe, increase to 10–20. Always validate the final ensemble with [X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring) to confirm that the guided ensemble improves the integrated score over the unguided baseline.

Sources: [model.py](idpforge/model.py#L258-L269), [sample_idp.py](sample_idp.py#L64-L86)

## Next Steps

- See [IDP Sampling (Fully Disordered)](12-idp-sampling-fully-disordered) for the complete sampling workflow that invokes these potentials.
- See [X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring) for quantitative validation of guided ensembles against experimental data.
- See [Configuration Reference](22-configuration-reference) for the full YAML schema including all potential parameters.

# AMBER Relaxation and Repair



IDPForge's AMBER Relaxation and Repair pipeline transforms raw diffusion outputs into physically plausible protein conformers through a three-phase protocol: **pre-relaxation screening**, **AMBER energy minimization**, and **structural repair with re-relaxation**. This pipeline is the critical bridge between the denoiser's atom37 coordinate predictions and the validated ensemble members that enter downstream scoring—every conformer must survive a cascade of geometric and stereochemical gates before earning a `_validated.pdb` suffix.

## Pipeline Architecture

The full pipeline executes as a sequential gate chain inside `output_to_pdb`, where each stage can reject a conformer before the next stage runs. Conformers that pass all gates are renamed from `_relaxed.pdb` to `_validated.pdb` and stamped as clean MODEL blocks for downstream consumption.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Raw atom37 from Denoiser"] --> B{"NaN Check"}
    B -->|has NaN| X1["SKIP"]
    B -->|clean| C{"Pre-Relax Backbone Continuity"}
    C -->|FAIL| X2["SKIP"]
    C -->|PASS| D["Write _raw.pdb"]
    E["AMBER Minimization<br/>(OpenMM + ff14SB)"]
    D --> E
    E -->|minimization failed| X3["REJECT"]
    E -->|success| F{"Violation Gate<br/>(ring-AA + free-set)"}
    F -->|violations exceed threshold| X4["REJECT"]
    F -->|PASS| G["Write _relaxed.pdb"]
    G --> H{"Bond Integrity Check"}
    H --> I["Chirality Repair<br/>(D→L flip)"]
    H --> J["Histidine Naming Fix"]
    I --> K{"Repairs Applied?"}
    J --> K
    K -->|Yes| L["Re-Relaxation"]
    K -->|No| M["Skip Re-Relax"]
    L --> N["Structural Validation"]
    M --> N
    O["Chirality / Bonds /<br/>Clashes / Topology"]
    N --> O
    O -->|FAIL| X5["DELETE _relaxed.pdb"]
    O -->|PASS| P{"Fold/Junction<br/>Curvature Gates"}
    P -->|FAIL| X6["DELETE"]
    P -->|PASS| Q["Rename to _validated.pdb"]
```

Sources: [misc.py](/idpforge/misc.py#L119-L470), [relax.py](/idpforge/utils/relax.py#L21-L92)

## Phase 1: Pre-Relaxation Screening

Before investing in expensive AMBER minimization, IDPForge applies a lightweight **backbone continuity filter** that catches geometrically impossible diffusion outputs early. The check walks every consecutive CA–CA pair along the chain and verifies the distance falls within one of two thresholds:

| Bond Type | CA–CA Threshold (Å) | Rationale |
|-----------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Backbone** (both residues same domain) | 9.12 | Tolerance for disordered backbone stretch |
| **Junction** (residues straddle fold/IDR boundary) | 6.46 | Tighter tolerance at the ordered–disordered interface |

A bond is classified as a junction when `viol_mask[i] ≠ viol_mask[i+1]`—that is, when the two adjacent residues belong to different domains (folded vs. IDR). Conformers failing any bond are silently discarded before PDB serialization, saving significant compute.

Sources: [pre_relax.py](/idpforge/utils/pre_relax.py#L1-L30), [misc.py](/idpforge/misc.py#L198-L237)

## Phase 2: AMBER Minimization and Violation Gating

### Energy Minimization

The core relaxation delegates to OpenFold's `AmberRelaxation` class, which wraps OpenMM with the AMBER ff14SB force field. The minimizer is configured through the `relax` section of the sampling YAML:

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `max_iterations` | 0 | Inner L-BFGS iteration cap (0 = OpenMM default) |
| `tolerance` | 10.0 | Energy convergence tolerance (kJ/mol) |
| `stiffness` | 10.0 | Positional restraint strength on folded residues |
| `max_outer_iterations` | 20 | Outer iteration limit for the restraint schedule |
| `exclude_residues` | `[]` | Residue indices excluded from positional restraints (populated at runtime from `~mask`) |

The critical design choice is the **positional restraint asymmetry**: folded-domain residues are held near their template coordinates by harmonic restraints (controlled by `stiffness`), while IDR residues (listed in `exclude_residues`) are free to move during minimization. This preserves the experimentally determined fold while allowing the disordered region to relax into a low-energy conformation.

Sources: [relax.py](/idpforge/utils/relax.py#L21-L42), [sample.yml](/configs/sample.yml#L51-L57), [sample_ldr.py](/idpforge/../sample_ldr.py#L99-L108)

### Violation Gates

After minimization, `relax_protein` applies two acceptance gates over the **free residue set** (IDR + junctions, defined by `viol_mask`):

**Ring-residue gate.** Aromatic residues (F, Y, W, H, P) are checked for steric violations. If the fraction of violated ring residues exceeds `viol_threshold` (default 2%), the conformer is rejected. This catches cases where AMBER could not resolve ring clashes—common at fold/IDR junctions where backbone strain propagates into sidechain geometry.

**Free-set violation gate.** The total violation count and fraction across all free residues are checked against both a fractional threshold and an absolute cap: `viol_cap = max(4, ⌈viol_threshold × n_free⌉)`. A conformer is rejected if either `viol_frac > viol_threshold` or `viol_total > viol_cap`. The dual criterion prevents a single bad residue from slipping through when the chain is long.

```python
# Dual rejection criterion from relax.py
viol_cap = max(4, int(np.ceil(viol_threshold * n_free)))
if viol_frac > viol_threshold or viol_total > viol_cap:
    # REJECT
```

Sources: [relax.py](/idpforge/utils/relax.py#L44-L76)

## Phase 3: Structural Repair

Even when AMBER minimization succeeds, two classes of systematic artifacts can survive: **D-amino acid chirality flips** and **histidine imidazole ring atom renaming**. Both are repaired in-place on the `_relaxed.pdb` file, and any repair triggers a mandatory re-relaxation to ensure the corrected geometry remains energy-consistent.

### Chirality Repair: D→L Isomer Reflection

AMBER's OpenMM backend can occasionally produce D-amino acid configurations, particularly for residues near high-strain junctions. The repair algorithm:

1. **Detection** uses the scalar triple product `vol = (v_N × v_C) · v_CB` computed from the N→CA, C→CA, and CB→CA vectors. Residues where `vol < 1.0` are flagged as D-isomers (the threshold of 1.0 rather than 0.0 provides margin for near-planar distortions). This mirrors the same check in `check_chirality` from `structure_validation.py`.
2. **Repair** reflects every **sidechain atom** across the N-CA-C plane. Backbone atoms (N, H, CA, HA2, HA3, C, O, OXT) are left untouched. The reflection formula for a sidechain atom at position `p` is: `p' = CA + v − 2(v·n̂)n̂`, where `v = p − CA` and `n̂` is the unit normal to the N-CA-C plane.

> [!TIP]
> The chirality repair reflects the full sidechain, not just CB. Partial reflection (CB-only) would leave CG, CD, etc. in the D-configuration, causing bond-length artifacts in subsequent re-relaxation.

Sources: [structure_repair.py](/idpforge/utils/structure_repair.py#L35-L153)

### Histidine Imidazole Ring Naming Repair

AMBER relaxation can scramble atom identities within the HIS imidazole ring (CG, ND1, CE1, NE2, CD2 and their hydrogens), especially at the HID/HIE/HIP protonation boundary. The repair is purely **geometric**—no chemical inference is needed:

1. **Find CG** as the sidechain atom closest to CB (~1.51 Å expected).
2. **Trace the five-membered ring** via bond-distance adjacency: atoms within 1.25–1.45 Å of each other form ring edges. A deterministic walk from CG constructs the ring order.
3. **Determine ring direction** by counting hydrogen neighbors per ring atom. The hydrogen-count pattern uniquely identifies the protonation state and orientation:
   - HID forward: `[1, 1, 0, 1]` (ND1 protonated)
   - HIE forward: `[0, 1, 1, 1]` (NE2 protonated)
   - HIP forward: `[1, 1, 1, 1]` (both protonated; CG–ND1 distance ~1.38 Å vs CG–CD2 ~1.35 Å breaks the tie)
4. **Reassign atom names** in the PDB file and rewrite the element column.

Sources: [structure_repair.py](/idpforge/utils/structure_repair.py#L156-L358)

## Repair-Triggered Re-Relaxation

When either `repair_chirality` or `fix_histidine_naming` makes corrections, the `needs_rerelax` flag is set and the conformer undergoes a second AMBER minimization pass. The re-relaxation workflow:

1. Reload the repaired PDB via `from_pdb_string`.
2. Delete the existing `_relaxed.pdb`.
3. Run `relax_protein` again with the same configuration (stiffness, exclude_residues, violation thresholds).
4. If re-relaxation fails or the violation gate rejects, the conformer is discarded entirely.

This two-pass protocol (relax → repair → re-relax) ensures that chirality flips and HIS renaming don't introduce new steric clashes or bond distortions that would only appear after the geometric correction.

Sources: [misc.py](/idpforge/misc.py#L308-L357), [relax_raw.py](/relax_raw.py#L127-L166)

## Standalone Relaxation: `relax_raw.py`

For post-hoc processing of existing raw PDB files, the `relax_raw.py` script provides the same relaxation and optional validation pipeline outside the sampling loop:

```bash
# Basic relaxation only
python relax_raw.py ./raw_conformers template.npz configs/sample.yml --cuda

# Full relax + repair + validate
python relax_raw.py ./raw_conformers template.npz configs/sample.yml \
    --cuda --validate --verbose

# Custom output directory
python relax_raw.py ./raw_conformers template.npz configs/sample.yml \
    --cuda --output_dir ./relaxed_conformers
```

The script loads the fold mask from the template `.npz` file (where `True` = folded, `False` = IDR), derives `exclude_residues` from `~mask`, and processes all `*_raw.pdb` files in sorted numerical order. With `--validate`, it runs the full repair + validation chain and produces `_validated.pdb` files for conformers that pass all gates.

Sources: [relax_raw.py](/relax_raw.py#L1-L232)

## File Lifecycle Summary

The pipeline produces a deterministic file naming convention that tracks each conformer's progress through the gates:

| Stage | Filename Pattern | Condition |
|-------|-----------------|-----------|
| Raw diffusion output | `{n}_raw.pdb` | Written after pre-relax screening passes |
| After AMBER relaxation | `{n}_relaxed.pdb` | Written if minimization + violation gate pass |
| After full validation | `{n}_validated.pdb` | Renamed from `_relaxed` if all gates pass |

Conformers that fail at any gate have their intermediate file deleted. The `_validated.pdb` suffix is the **contract** that downstream consumers ([X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring), AlphaFlex stitching) rely on—it guarantees the conformer has survived the complete geometric, stereochemical, and topological validation chain.

> [!TIP]
> When using `--no_relax` in `sample_ldr.py`, the search pattern switches from `*_validated.pdb` to `*_raw.pdb`. Downstream scripts that glob for `*_validated.pdb` will find zero files—always pair `--no_relax` with a subsequent `relax_raw.py --validate` run.

Sources: [misc.py](/idpforge/misc.py#L451-L465), [sample_ldr.py](/sample_ldr.py#L100-L108)

## Next Steps

The validated conformers produced by this pipeline become the input to the [Structure Validation Pipeline](16-structure-validation-pipeline) (which provides the detailed four-axis validation logic) and ultimately feed into [X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring) for experimental reweighting.

# Structure Validation Pipeline



The Structure Validation Pipeline is IDPForge's multi-stage quality gate that transforms raw diffusion outputs into physically credible protein conformers. It operates as a **four-phase filter cascade** — pre-relaxation screening, AMBER relaxation with violation gates, structural validation, and optional fold-integrity gates — each stage progressively eliminating geometrically or topologically defective structures. The pipeline is not a single function but an orchestrated workflow embedded in the sampling loop, where conformers that fail any gate are silently discarded and replaced by new diffusion samples until the target ensemble size is reached.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L1-L725), [misc.py](idpforge/misc.py#L119-L200)

## Pipeline Architecture

The validation pipeline executes as a sequential gate chain within `output_to_pdb`, the central orchestrator called by both [IDP Sampling (Fully Disordered)](12-idp-sampling-fully-disordered) and [IDR Sampling with Folded Templates](13-idr-sampling-with-folded-templates). Each gate can reject a conformer early (fail-fast), preventing wasted computation on structures that are already unsalvageable. The diagram below shows the complete flow from raw diffusion output to validated PDB:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Raw Diffusion Output<br>(atom37 coordinates)"] --> B{"NaN Check"}
    B -->|Fail| X["Discard"]
    B -->|Pass| C{"Backbone Continuity<br>(Pre-Relax)"}
    C -->|Fail| X
    C -->|Pass| D["Write Raw PDB"]
    D --> E["AMBER Relaxation<br>(relax.py)"]
    E -->|Minimization Failed| X
    E -->|Relaxed| F{"Ring-AA Violation Gate"}
    F -->|Fail| X
    F -->|Pass| G{"Free-Residue Violation Gate"}
    G -->|Fail| X
    G -->|Pass| H["Pre-Validation Repair<br>(structure_repair.py)"]
    H --> I{"Chirality Check"}
    I -->|Fail| X
    I -->|Pass| J{"Bond Integrity Check"}
    J -->|Fail| X
    J -->|Pass| K{"Clash Score Check"}
    K -->|Fail| X
    K -->|Pass| L{"Knot Topology Check<br>(AlphaKnot2 Hybrid)"}
    L -->|Fail| X
    L -->|Pass| M{"Fold-Integrity Gates<br>(IDR only)"}
    M -->|Fail| X
    M -->|Pass| N["Write _validated.pdb"]

    style X fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff
    style N fill:#51cf66,color:#fff
```

The fail-fast behavior is controlled by the `full_report` parameter in `validate_structure_post_relax`. When `full_report=False` (the default), the function returns immediately upon the first failure, producing a minimal diagnostic. When `full_report=True`, all checks run to completion and the info dict contains results for every gate regardless of intermediate failures.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L583-L724), [misc.py](idpforge/misc.py#L119-L200)

## Phase 1: Pre-Relaxation Screening

Before any expensive AMBER minimization, a lightweight **backbone continuity filter** rejects conformers with broken peptide chains. This check operates directly on the CA-CA distances from the diffusion output, requiring no PDB I/O or OpenMM topology construction.

The function `check_backbone_continuity` distinguishes two distance thresholds:

| Segment Type | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Junction** (IDR↔Folded boundary) | 6.46 Å | Looser: the IDR-to-folded anchor transition is inherently flexible |
| **Backbone** (within same domain) | 9.12 Å | Stricter: consecutive CA atoms within a continuous domain should be close |

A junction is identified wherever adjacent residues differ in their violation mask (i.e., one is in the folded domain and the other in the IDR). Non-sequential residue indices (gaps in `residue_index`) are skipped. The function returns a boolean pass/fail alongside per-bond details for debugging.

Sources: [pre_relax.py](idpforge/utils/pre_relax.py#L1-L30)

## Phase 2: AMBER Relaxation and Violation Gates

After passing pre-relaxation screening, the raw coordinates are written to a PDB file and submitted to OpenMM's AMBER relaxation. The relaxation step itself is documented in [AMBER Relaxation and Repair](15-amber-relaxation-and-repair); here we focus on the **acceptance gates** that the relaxed structure must satisfy.

### Ring-Amino-Acid Violation Gate

Ring-containing residues (F, Y, W, H, P) are geometrically constrained — AMBER cannot freely rotate their planar groups. If too many ring residues remain violated after minimization, the conformer is rejected:

```
ring_violated / n_ring_total > viol_threshold  →  REJECT
```

The default `viol_threshold` is 0.02 (2%), meaning even a few distorted ring residues trigger rejection. This gate catches cases where the diffusion output placed side chains in sterically impossible configurations that relaxation cannot resolve.

### Free-Residue Violation Gate

The "free" residue set is the union of the IDR and junction residues (i.e., everything not positionally restrained during relaxation). Two conditions must both hold:

| Condition | Formula | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Fraction gate** | `viol_frac ≤ viol_threshold` | Global quality: few residues remain distorted |
| **Count cap** | `viol_total ≤ max(4, ⌈threshold × n_free⌉)` | Absolute cap prevents large IDRs from passing with many small violations |

Sources: [relax.py](idpforge/utils/relax.py#L21-L92)

## Phase 3: Post-Relaxation Structural Validation

The core validation function `validate_structure_post_relax` runs four independent checks on the relaxed OpenMM topology and positions. Each check is timed independently, and results are accumulated into an info dictionary.

### Chirality Check

The chirality check detects **D-amino acids** — residues where the side chain has been reflected across the N–CA–C backbone plane. For each non-glycine residue, it computes the **scalar triple product** of the vectors from CA to N, C, and CB:

$$V = (\vec{v_N} \times \vec{v_C}) \cdot \vec{v_{CB}}$$

| Volume | Classification | Action |
|---|---|---|
| V ≥ 1.0 | L-amino acid (correct) | Pass |
| 0 < V < 1.0 | Planar/Distorted | Flag as issue |
| V < 0 | D-amino acid (inverted) | Flag as issue |

Glycine is exempted (achiral). A volume threshold of 1.0 (rather than 0.0) provides a safety margin against near-planar distortions that, while technically L-configured, indicate severe geometric stress.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L99-L119)

### Bond Integrity Check

The bond integrity check operates in two modes — **intra-residue** and **inter-residue** — using a geometry/graph hybrid approach that is atom-name agnostic:

**Intra-residue**: For each residue, the check compares the *expected* heavy-atom bond degree sequence (from the OpenMM topology graph) against the *observed* degree sequence (from distance-based neighbor counting with a 2.0 Å covalent cutoff). If the sorted degree sequences disagree and the observed graph has fewer bonds or disconnected atoms, the residue is flagged. Specific stretched bonds are identified by measuring distances along the topology's explicit bond edges.

**Inter-residue**: Each heavy-atom bond that crosses residue boundaries is checked directly: if the inter-atomic distance exceeds the `threshold` (default 2.2 Å), the bond is reported as broken with the measured distance.

This dual strategy catches both *graph topology changes* (atoms disconnected by large displacements) and *specific bond stretches* (known bonds whose lengths exceed physical limits).

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L121-L207)

### Clash Score Check

The clash detection uses a **cKDTree-accelerated backbone-backbone overlap** calculation. Only N, CA, and C atoms are considered, using element-specific van der Waals radii:

| Element | VdW Radius (Å) |
|---|---|
| C | 1.70 |
| N | 1.55 |
| O | 1.52 |
| S | 1.80 |
| P | 1.80 |
| H | 1.20 |

The tree queries all pairs within 4.0 Å and filters them through three exclusion rules applied in sequence:

1. **Chain/bond exclusion**: Adjacent residues (|Δres_id| ≤ 1) on the same chain are excluded — their close contact is the expected peptide backbone
2. **Domain logic** (IDR mode): When `idr_start` and `idr_end` are provided, pairs where *both* atoms lie in the folded domain are excluded — only IDR-involved clashes are penalized, since folded-domain contacts are expected
3. **Overlap calculation**: `overlap = (r_i + r_j) - distance`; flagged when `overlap ≥ overlap_cutoff` (default 0.4 Å)

The final clash score is normalized as `(clash_count / n_backbone_atoms) × 1000`, and the conformer passes if the score is at or below `strict_clash_threshold` (default 10.0).

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L209-L269)

### Knot Topology Check (AlphaKnot2 Hybrid)

The topology check uses a **two-phase Alexander→HOMFLY hybrid** classifier that balances speed against rigor. The pipeline supports both **global** (full-chain) and **per-domain** knot classification, selected by whether `expected_knot_type` is a list of domain specs or a single value.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Extract CA coordinates"] --> B["Phase 1: Alexander Polynomial<br/>(100 probabilistic closures)"]
    B --> C{"P(Unknot) ≥ 0.65?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Label: None<br/>(High-Confidence Unknot)"]
    C -->|No| E["Phase 2: HOMFLY-PT Polynomial<br/>(Mass-Center closure)"]
    E --> F{"HOMFLY = Unknot?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["Label: None<br/>(Confirmed by HOMFLY)"]
    F -->|No| H["Label: Knot<br/>(type extracted from HOMFLY)"]

    style D fill:#51cf66,color:#fff
    style G fill:#51cf66,color:#fff
    style H fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fff
```

**Phase 1 — Alexander polynomial** is computed with 100 probabilistic closures (`ALEXANDER_TRIES = 100`). If the probability of unknot exceeds `ALPHAKNOT_P_UNKNOT_MAX = 0.65`, the structure is classified as unknotted with high confidence and HOMFLY is skipped entirely, saving significant compute.

**Phase 2 — HOMFLY-PT polynomial** is invoked only when the Alexander result is ambiguous (the "gray zone" where P(Unknot) < 0.65). HOMFLY-PT is a more powerful knot invariant that can distinguish knot types the Alexander polynomial cannot. It uses `Closure.MASS_CENTER` for deterministic closure.

**Per-domain classification** is triggered when `expected_knot_type` is a list of domain specifications (loaded from `knot_screening.json`). Each domain's CA coordinates are extracted and classified independently. A conformer passes if every domain's detected knot type matches its expected type (where `null`/`None` means unknot).

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L274-L452), [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L636-L707)

### Composite Validation Result

The main entry point `validate_structure_post_relax` orchestrates all four checks and produces a composite result:

```python
all_pass, info = validate_structure_post_relax(
    topology, positions, pdb_path="",
    strict_clash_threshold=10.0,
    idr_start=None, idr_end=None,
    expected_knot_type=None,
    full_report=False
)
```

| Return Value | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `all_pass` | `bool` | `True` only if all four gates pass |
| `info["chirality_pass"]` | `bool` | No D-amino acids detected |
| `info["bonds_pass"]` | `bool` | No broken intra/inter-residue bonds |
| `info["clash_pass"]` | `bool` | Clash score ≤ threshold |
| `info["knot_pass"]` | `bool` | Topology matches expectation |
| `info["reason"]` | `str` | `"OK"` if all pass; comma-separated failure labels otherwise |

Each check's runtime is recorded in `info` (e.g., `Time_Chirality_s`, `Time_Bonds_s`, `Time_Clashes_s`, `Time_Knots_s`), enabling performance profiling of the validation pipeline.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L583-L724)

## Phase 4: Fold-Integrity Gates (IDR Sampling Only)

For [IDR Sampling with Folded Templates](13-idr-sampling-with-folded-templates), two additional geometric gates protect the structural integrity of the folded domain and its junctions with the IDR. These gates are **superposition-free** — they operate entirely on intrinsic geometric quantities (curvature, distance matrices) that are invariant to rigid-body motions, avoiding the fragility of RMSD-based thresholds.

### Junction Curvature Gate

The junction curvature gate rejects conformers where the IDR has been **pulled taut** to reach the folded anchor — a common failure mode where the diffusion process stretches the IDR into an unnaturally straight bridge. It computes discrete backbone curvature κ per residue:

$$\kappa_i = \frac{2 \sin(\theta_i / 2)}{|\mathbf{r}_{i+1} - \mathbf{r}_{i-1}|}$$

where θ_i is the angle at CA_i between the incoming and outgoing CA–CA vectors. CA–CA distances exceeding 4.5 Å are treated as chain breaks and excluded. The gate examines a window of 20 residues on the IDR side of each junction and requires the mean curvature to meet a minimum threshold (`junction_kappa`, default 0.0 = disabled).

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L488-L530)

### Fold Curvature Gate

The fold curvature gate rejects conformers where junction-adjacent **folded residues** have been straightened — indicating the IDR sampling has distorted the fixed template. For each junction, it compares the mean curvature in a window (default 15 residues) of the model against the reference template:

$$\frac{\bar{\kappa}_{\text{model}}}{\bar{\kappa}_{\text{ref}}} \geq \texttt{fold\_curv\_ratio}$$

The gate is only applied when the reference curvature in the window exceeds `min_ref_kappa` (0.03 Å⁻¹), avoiding penalization of naturally straight template regions. This ratio-based criterion is rigid-motion invariant and directly measures whether the fold has been flattened relative to its native geometry.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L533-L576)

### Folded CA-lDDT Gate

A superposition-free **CA-lDDT quality gate** assesses local distance accuracy over the folded region. For all residue pairs within an inclusion radius (15 Å) in the reference, it computes the fraction of pairs where the distance difference falls within multiple thresholds (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 Å). The lDDT score is the mean across these thresholds, and the conformer passes if the score meets the configured `threshold`.

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L458-L485)

## Pre-Validation Structural Repair

Before the post-relaxation validation checks run, two repair operations are applied to fix common AMBER relaxation artifacts:

### Chirality Repair

When `check_chirality` detects D-amino acids, `repair_chirality` reflects all sidechain atoms across the **N–CA–C plane** to restore the L-isomer geometry. The reflection is computed as:

$$\mathbf{p}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{CA} + \vec{v} - 2(\vec{v} \cdot \hat{n})\hat{n}$$

where **v** is the vector from CA to the sidechain atom and **n̂** is the unit normal of the N–CA–C plane. Backbone atoms (N, H, CA, HA2, HA3, C, O, OXT) are held fixed during reflection. The repair operates by direct PDB line editing, avoiding a full write-parse cycle.

Sources: [structure_repair.py](idpforge/utils/structure_repair.py#L35-L153)

### Histidine Ring Naming Repair

AMBER relaxation can **scramble atom identities** within the histidine imidazole ring, swapping heavy-atom and hydrogen labels (e.g., ND1↔CD2). The `fix_histidine_naming` function reassigns atom names based purely on spatial geometry through a five-step algorithm:

1. **Find CG**: the sidechain atom closest to CB (~1.51 Å)
2. **Trace the five-membered ring** via bond-distance adjacency (1.25–1.45 Å bonds)
3. **Count hydrogen neighbors** per ring atom (N–H bonds ≤ 1.15 Å)
4. **Determine ring direction** from the hydrogen-count pattern (HID: [1,1,0,1], HIE: [0,1,1,1], HIP: [1,1,1,1])
5. **Rewrite PDB atom names** and element symbols for all mismatched ring atoms and their hydrogens

Sources: [structure_repair.py](idpforge/utils/structure_repair.py#L156-L358)

## Validation Metrics

The `validation_metrics` module provides ensemble-level quality metrics used by the [X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring) pipeline:

| Function | Input | Output | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `calc_rg_with_mask` | CA coords `[batch, nres, 3]`, mask `[batch, nres]` | Rg `[batch]` | Radius of gyration over valid (masked) residues |
| `rg_dist_per_group` | Predicted coords, true Rg values, sequences, mask | Scalar | Mean absolute Rg divergence grouped by sequence identity |

These metrics enable comparison of predicted ensemble properties against experimental observables without requiring residue-level alignment.

Sources: [validation_metrics.py](idpforge/utils/validation_metrics.py#L1-L54)

## Integration with Sampling Loops

The validation pipeline is embedded in the `output_to_pdb` function, which is the single exit point from the diffusion model into the filesystem. Both sampling scripts call it identically:

```python
# In sample_idp.py — fully disordered proteins
output_to_pdb(outputs, relax=relax_opts,
    save_path=abs_output_dir, counter=start_idx,
    counter_cap=nsample, verbose=verbose)

# In sample_ldr.py — IDR with folded template
output_to_pdb(outputs, relax=relax_opts,
    save_path=abs_output_dir, counter=start_idx,
    counter_cap=nsample, viol_mask=~fold_data["mask"],
    fold_ref_ca=fold_ref_ca, fold_mask=fold_data["mask"],
    fold_curv_ratio=fold_curv_ratio,
    fold_curv_window=fold_curv_window,
    junction_kappa=junction_kappa,
    expected_knot_type=expected_knot_type)
```

The sampling loop continues until `count_done()` — the number of `*_validated.pdb` files on disk — reaches the target `nsample`. Rejected conformers are simply not written, and the loop generates new diffusion samples to replace them. The `*_raw.pdb` files (written before relaxation) are retained for debugging, while only `*_validated.pdb` files count toward the ensemble target.

> [!TIP]
> The validation pipeline is designed as a **reject-only filter** — it never modifies conformers in-place (except for the pre-validation chirality and histidine repairs). This means the acceptance rate directly controls sampling efficiency: if too many conformers are rejected, increase `nsample` or loosen thresholds rather than attempting to patch individual structures.

> [!TIP]
> When sampling IDRs with knotted folded domains, always provide `--expected_knot_type` as a per-domain JSON spec. Without it, the legacy full-chain unknot baseline will reject any conformer where the entire chain (including the knot) is not globally unknotted — incorrectly discarding valid structures with native knots.

Sources: [sample_idp.py](sample_idp.py#L158-L160), [sample_ldr.py](sample_ldr.py#L207-L218)

## Gate Configuration Summary

| Gate | Parameter | Default | Scope | Disable By |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NaN coordinates | — | Always on | Both | Cannot disable |
| Backbone continuity | — | Always on | Both | `--no_relax` (skips entirely) |
| Ring-AA violation | `viol_threshold` | 0.02 | Both | Set threshold to 1.0 |
| Free-residue violation | `viol_threshold` | 0.02 | Both | Set threshold to 1.0 |
| Chirality | — | Always on | Both | Cannot disable |
| Bond integrity | `threshold` | 2.2 Å | Both | Cannot disable |
| Clash score | `strict_clash_threshold` | 10.0 | Both | Set to ∞ |
| Knot topology | `expected_knot_type` | None (global unknot) | Both | Pass `[]` (empty list) |
| Junction curvature | `--junction_kappa` | 0.0 (off) | IDR only | Leave at 0.0 |
| Fold curvature | `--fold_curv_ratio` | 0.0 (off) | IDR only | Leave at 0.0 |
| Folded CA-lDDT | `threshold` | Config-dependent | IDR only | Set to 0.0 |

Sources: [structure_validation.py](idpforge/utils/structure_validation.py#L583-L590), [sample_ldr.py](sample_ldr.py#L248-L261)

## Next Steps

After validation, accepted conformers proceed to ensemble-level quality assessment:

- **[X-EISD Ensemble Scoring](17-x-eisd-ensemble-scoring)**: Score and rank the validated ensemble against experimental data using Bayesian integration
- **[AMBER Relaxation and Repair](15-amber-relaxation-and-repair)**: Deeper details on the AMBER minimization configuration and restraint strategies that precede validation
- **[Configuration Reference](22-configuration-reference)**: Complete parameter specifications for all validation thresholds

# X-EISD Ensemble Scoring



**X-EISD** (Cross-Ensemble Information Score Difference) is IDPForge's maximum log-likelihood framework for scoring intrinsically disordered protein ensembles against experimental observables. It back-calculates NMR and FRET observables from PDB structures, analytically optimizes error-model parameters per property, and computes ensemble-level log-likelihoods that enable rigorous, cross-method benchmarking of conformational ensembles. The pipeline supports five observable types—**J-couplings**, **chemical shifts**, **NOE distances**, **PRE distances**, and **FRET efficiencies**—and provides both a stochastic sub-sampling protocol (30 trials × 100 conformers) and deterministic single-pass scoring, with optional Monte Carlo ensemble optimization and Eq. S11 cross-method normalization for publication-ready benchmark tables.

Sources: [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py#L1-L171), [scoring/scorer.py](/scoring/scorer.py#L1-L136)

## Architecture Overview

The scoring system is organized as a layered pipeline within the `scoring/` package, with [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py) serving as the CLI entry point. Each module owns a distinct computational responsibility: **parser** resolves experimental data and back-calculation uncertainties, **calculator** forward-models observables from 3D structures, **scorer** computes per-property log-likelihoods with analytically optimal error parameters, **optimizer** orchestrates multi-property scoring and optional Metropolis–Hastings ensemble selection, and **normalize**/**rg** produce cross-method benchmark tables and radius-of-gyration statistics.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CLI["score_ensemble.py  (Entry Point)"]
        A["argparse: protname, pdbpath, --jc/--cs/--noe/--pre/--fret"]
        B["Mode dispatch: default | --all | --rg | --normalize"]
    end

    subgraph Parser["scoring/parser.py"]
        C["EXP_DATA_LIB: lazy protein→{dtype: file} registry"]
        D["Stack: (name, data, sigma, mu)"]
        E["read_bc_data: attach BC_ERRORS per property"]
    end

    subgraph Calculator["scoring/calculator.py"]
        F["jc_backcalc:  φ dihedral → cos(φ-60°)"]
        G["cshift_backcalc: CSpred subprocess (parallel)"]
        H["noe_backcalc: ⟨r⁻⁶⟩⁻¹ᐟ⁶ averaging"]
        I["pre_backcalc: single-atom distance"]
        J["fret_backcalc: 1/(1+(d/R₀)⁶)"]
        K["calc_rg: mass-weighted Rg"]
    end

    subgraph Scorer["scoring/scorer.py"]
        L["calc_opt_params: σ²/(1+σ²/σ_exp²) · (exp-β)"]
        M["normal_loglike: -γ(x-μ)²/2σ²"]
        N["calc_score: f_q + f_err"]
        O["Property-specific scorers: jc, cs, noe, pre, fret"]
    end

    subgraph Optimizer["scoring/optimizer.py"]
        P["XEISD.calc_scores: aggregate multi-property"]
        Q["XEISD.optimize: Metropolis–Hastings swap"]
        R["monte_carlo: log-domain acceptance"]
    end

    subgraph PostProc["Post-Processing"]
        S["normalize.py: Eq. S11 per-protein normalization"]
        T["rg.py: ⟨Rg⟩ trials + %|ΔRg|/Rg"]
    end

    A --> C
    B --> F & G & H & I & J
    C --> D --> E
    F & G & H & I & J --> D
    D --> L --> M --> N --> O
    O --> P --> Q
    P --> S & T
    R --> Q
```

Sources: [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py#L1-L171), [scoring/parser.py](/scoring/parser.py#L1-L81), [scoring/calculator.py](/scoring/calculator.py#L1-L250), [scoring/scorer.py](/scoring/scorer.py#L1-L136), [scoring/optimizer.py](/scoring/optimizer.py#L1-L108)

## The X-EISD Scoring Model

The core insight behind X-EISD is that **back-calculated observables from an ensemble carry two independent sources of uncertainty**: the intrinsic back-calculation error (σ_bc) from the forward model, and the experimental measurement error (σ_exp). Rather than treating these as fixed weights, X-EISD analytically derives **optimal latent correction parameters** that maximize the joint log-likelihood of both error models simultaneously. For a generic observable with ensemble-averaged back-calculation β, experimental value μ_exp, and correction parameter θ, the score decomposes as:

**log P = log N(θ; 0, σ_bc) + log N(μ_exp − θ − β; 0, σ_exp)**

The optimal θ* is found in closed form as `θ* = (σ²_bc / σ²_exp) · (μ_exp − β) / (1 + σ²_bc/σ²_exp)`, which reduces to the experimental residual when back-calculation is much more precise than experiment (σ_bc ≪ σ_exp), and to zero when the opposite holds. This Bayesian treatment avoids arbitrary weighting between data sources and yields a principled, additive log-likelihood across all observables.

Sources: [scoring/scorer.py](/scoring/scorer.py#L6-L46)

### Property-Specific Scoring Functions

Each experimental observable type requires a tailored scoring function due to differences in how ensemble averaging is performed and how the error model is parameterized:

| Observable | Ensemble Average | Error Parameters | Scoring Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **J-couplings (JC)** | ⟨cos(φ−60°)⟩, ⟨cos²(φ−60°)⟩ | A, B, C with fixed μ, σ from Karplus calibration | `jc_score_ensemble` — 3D quadratic solve for (A\*, B\*, C\*) |
| **Chemical shifts (CS)** | ⟨δ_atom⟩ per atom type | Per-atom σ_bc (C: 1.31, CA: 0.97, N: 2.16, …) | `cs_score_ensemble` — per-shift θ\*, with χ² diagnostics |
| **NOE distances** | ⟨r⁻⁶⟩⁻¹ᐟ⁶ (r⁻⁶-weighted) | σ_bc = 0.01 Å | `dist_score_ensemble` — asymmetric bounds (upper/lower) |
| **PRE distances** | Single-atom distance | σ_bc = 0.001 Å | `dist_score_ensemble` — shared with NOE |
| **FRET efficiency** | ⟨1/(1+(d/R₀)⁶)⟩ | σ_bc = 0.0074 | `generic_score_ensemble` — standard Gaussian |

For **J-couplings**, the Karplus relation J = A·cos²(φ−60°) + B·cos(φ−60°) + C makes the log-likelihood a function of three Karplus parameters (A, B, C) rather than a single correction parameter. The optimizer solves a 3×3 linear system per coupling to find the jointly optimal (A\*, B\*, C\*), then evaluates the sum of four Gaussian log-likelihoods: one for each Karplus parameter's deviation from its calibrated mean, plus the experimental residual. For **NOE/PRE distances**, the scoring accounts for asymmetric experimental bounds by computing the minimum absolute error across three trial deviations (center, upper-bound, lower-bound).

Sources: [scoring/scorer.py](/scoring/scorer.py#L48-L136), [scoring/parser.py](/scoring/parser.py#L15-L22)

## Back-Calculation Engine

The back-calculation layer transforms PDB coordinates into predicted experimental observables. Each function operates over the full ensemble of structures and returns a matrix of shape `(n_conformers, n_observations)` that feeds into the scorer.

**J-coupling back-calculation** extracts the backbone φ dihedral angle at each residue specified in the experimental data file, then computes cos(φ − 60°) as the Karplus-relevant quantity. This uses Biopython's `calc_dihedral` on the C(i−1)–N(i)–CA(i)–C(i) atoms. **NOE distance back-calculation** computes the r⁻⁶-weighted ensemble average ⟨r⁻⁶⟩⁻¹ᐟ⁶ across all atom-pair assignments for each NOE, handling ambiguous assignments (e.g., HB2/HB3 → CB) via the `hydrogen_abbrev` and `heavy_atom_hydrogen` lookup tables. **PRE back-calculation** uses the same `_dist_backcalc` infrastructure but takes only the first atom-pair distance (no r⁻⁶ averaging). **FRET back-calculation** computes the Förster efficiency 1/(1+(d/R₀)⁶) for each labeled residue pair using the per-pair scale factor R₀ from the experimental data.

**Chemical shift back-calculation** is the most computationally expensive step and runs **CSpred (UCBShift) as an external subprocess** with up to 8 parallel workers via `ProcessPoolExecutor`. The subprocess isolation (configurable via `CSPRED_PYTHON` and `CSPRED_PATH` environment variables) accommodates CSpred's separate Python environment. Results are cached to `{property}_cache.csv` to avoid re-computation on subsequent runs.

Sources: [scoring/calculator.py](/scoring/calculator.py#L1-L250)

### Hydrogen-Atom Mapping

When experimental data references hydrogen atoms that are absent from relaxed PDB structures, the calculator falls back to heavy-atom proxies via two mapping dictionaries. The `hydrogen_abbrev` dictionary expands grouped hydrogen names (e.g., `HB → [HB2, HB3]` for ALA, `HD → [HD11, HD12, HD13, HD21, HD22, HD23]` for LEU) across all 20 amino acids. The `heavy_atom_hydrogen` dictionary maps hydrogen groups to their parent heavy atoms (e.g., `HB → [CB]`, `HD → [CD1, CD2]` for PHE) for the `--heavy-atom-substitute` mode. Both dictionaries are essential for accurate NOE/PRE back-calculation on AMBER-relaxed structures where explicit hydrogens may be stripped.

Sources: [scoring/calculator.py](/scoring/calculator.py#L58-L117)

## Experimental Data Registry

The `parser` module manages the interface between raw experimental data files and the scoring pipeline. The **`EXP_DATA_LIB`** singleton is a lazy-initialized dictionary mapping protein names to `{data_type: file_path}`. It discovers experimental files under the `$IDPFORGE_EXP_DATA` directory (default `Data/exp/`) following the naming convention `{protein}_{type}_exp.txt`. Each file is a CSV with columns specific to its observable type (e.g., `resnum, value, error` for JC; `res1, atom1, res2, atom2, dist_value, lower, upper` for PRE/NOE; `resnum, atomname, value, error` for CS; `res1, res2, scale` for FRET).

The **`read_bc_data`** function wraps raw back-calculation output into a `Stack` object that carries the computed data matrix alongside property-specific back-calculation uncertainties from the `BC_ERRORS` dictionary. For J-couplings, this includes both σ values (√0.14, √0.03, √0.08 for Karplus A, B, C) and μ values (6.51, −1.76, 1.6). For chemical shifts, the uncertainty is a per-atom-type dictionary (C: 1.31, CA: 0.97, H: 0.38, N: 2.16, etc.) derived from UCBShift validation statistics.

Sources: [scoring/parser.py](/scoring/parser.py#L1-L81)

## The XEISD Optimizer Class

The `XEISD` class in [optimizer.py](/scoring/optimizer.py) is the central orchestrator that aggregates per-property scores and optionally performs **Metropolis–Hastings ensemble optimization**. It is initialized with the full experimental data dictionary and the pre-computed back-calculation `Stack` objects, then exposes two primary methods:

**`calc_scores(dtypes, indices)`** evaluates the log-likelihood for a specific ensemble subset defined by `indices`. For each requested data type, it dispatches to the corresponding function in `ENSEMBLE_Scorers`, collecting both the MAE (mean absolute error) and the total log-likelihood score. For chemical shifts specifically, it additionally computes per-atom-type MAE, per-atom-type χ², and the overall χ²_CS diagnostic (Eq. 12 in the supplementary information): `χ² = (1/N) Σ (δ_exp − δ_bc)² / σ²_bc,atom`.

**`optimize(opt_props, ens_size, beta, ...)`** performs stochastic ensemble selection via single-structure swaps with Metropolis acceptance. Starting from a random initial ensemble of `ens_size` conformers, each iteration (default: 5 × pool_size) randomly replaces one conformer with another from the full pool, accepts the swap if the total log-likelihood improves (greedy mode, `opt_type='max'`) or with Metropolis probability `min(1, exp(β · Δ_score))` (Monte Carlo mode, `opt_type='mc'`). The `monte_carlo` helper implements **log-domain acceptance** to avoid overflow when probabilities exceed floating-point range, falling back to `exp(β · Δ_score)` comparison when both old and new probabilities are finite. The optimizer tracks visited configurations in `self.visited` to avoid redundant recomputation and returns the best-scoring ensemble indices, their per-property scores, and per-conformer statistics (mean and std of total score across all visits).

Sources: [scoring/optimizer.py](/scoring/optimizer.py#L1-L108)

## Ensemble Scoring Protocol

The default scoring protocol in `main()` implements the benchmark-standard procedure: **30 independent trials of 100-conformer random subsamples** drawn with replacement from the full pool of relaxed PDB structures. This stochastic evaluation accounts for the dependence of ensemble-averaged observables on the specific conformer selection, yielding mean and standard deviation statistics that quantify ensemble reproducibility.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Discover PDBs\n(*_relax*.pdb → *.pdb)"] --> B["Validate structures\n(Biopython parse)"]
    B --> C[Back-calculate\nall observables]
    C --> D[Compute Rg\nper conformer]
    D --> E{"--all flag?"}
    E -->|Yes| F[Single pass:\nall N conformers\n→ scores_all.csv]
    E -->|No| G["30 trials × 100 subsamples\n→ scores_trials.csv"]
    F --> H[Report\nmean ± stdev]
    G --> H
```

The pipeline discovers PDB files by searching for `*_relax*.pdb` first (post-[AMBER Relaxation](15-amber-relaxation-and-repair) structures), then falling back to `traj_pdbs/*_relax*.pdb`, then `*.pdb`. Invalid structures (those failing Biopython parsing or with empty chain A) are filtered out with warnings. Chemical shift back-calculations are cached to `cs_cache.csv` and restored on subsequent runs to avoid the expensive CSpred subprocess. Each trial produces a row in the output CSV with columns `{prop}_mae`, `{prop}_score` for each observable type, plus `rg` (mean ensemble Rg) and detailed CS diagnostics (`cs_{atom}_mae`, `cs_{atom}_chi2`, `cs_chi2`).

Sources: [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py#L44-L121)

### CLI Reference

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `protname pdbpath` | Protein name (must match `EXP_DATA_LIB` key) and path to PDB directory |
| `--jc / --cs / --noe / --pre / --fret` | Select observable types to score (any combination) |
| `--all` | Score every conformer in a single pass → `scores_all.csv` |
| `--ens-size N` | Subsample size per trial (default: 100) |
| `--trials N` | Number of random subsamples (default: 30) |
| `--force` | Re-score even if output CSV exists |
| `--normalize` | Build Eq. S11 cross-method benchmark table from existing scores |
| `--rg` | Compute per-ensemble Rg → `rg_trials.csv` |
| `--ens-base DIR` | Base directory with `{method}/{protein}/` hierarchy (for `--normalize`/`--rg`) |
| `--score-file FILE` | Per-protein score CSV to aggregate (default: `scores_trials.csv`) |
| `--exclude-methods M1,M2` | Drop specific method directories from the benchmark |
| `--proteins P1,P2` | Restrict to a protein subset |
| `--rg-json FILE` | Experimental Rg JSON for `%|ΔRg|/Rg` column |
| `--exp-dir DIR` | Override experimental data directory |

Sources: [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py#L124-L171)

## Cross-Method Benchmark Normalization

The `--normalize` mode produces the paper-style benchmark table (Eq. S11) that enables fair comparison across ensemble generation methods. It operates on a directory hierarchy `{ens_base}/{method}/{protein}/{score_file}` where each method directory (e.g., `idpforge`, `flexserv`, `md`) contains per-protein subdirectories with pre-computed `scores_trials.csv` files.

The normalization proceeds in three stages. First, **canonical protein sets** are derived for each observable category by scanning the experimental data directory: CS, JC, NOE, PRE, FRET, and the merged NOE/PRE union. Second, **raw score tables** (method × protein) are built by extracting the mean log-likelihood per category from each method's score CSVs. NOE and PRE scores are summed into a single NOE/PRE column. Third, **per-protein min-max normalization** is applied: `X_norm = (X − X_min) / (X_max − X_min)`, where X_min and X_max are computed across methods for each protein independently, ensuring that differences in score ranges across proteins do not dominate the aggregate ranking.

The output benchmark table includes seven columns: **Total** (normalized aggregate of CS + JC + NOE/PRE per protein, then averaged), **CS**, **JC**, **NOE/PRE** (individual category means), **FRET** (shown separately since few proteins have FRET data), **χ²_CS** (mean chemical shift χ² per method, lower is better), and **%|ΔRg|/Rg** (flat-bottom Rg deviation with tolerance σ_rg: `max(|Rg − Rg_exp| − σ_rg, 0) / Rg_exp × 100`). All intermediate tables (raw, normalized, per-category) are saved as CSVs for downstream analysis.

Sources: [scoring/normalize.py](/scoring/normalize.py#L1-L208)

## Radius of Gyration Pipeline

The `--rg` mode computes mass-weighted Rg for all atoms (including hydrogens) of chain A across the method/protein ensemble hierarchy. It supports both the trial-based protocol (30 trials × 100 subsamples → `rg_trials.csv`) and per-frame computation (`--all` → `rg.csv`). The implementation uses a pure-Python PDB parser (no Biopython dependency) for speed, extracting coordinates directly from ATOM/HETATM records with element identification from the PDB element column (positions 77–78) or the first alphabetic character in the atom name.

A critical design choice is the **deterministic seed per (method, protein) pair**, computed as `SHA1("{method}/{protein}")[:8]` interpreted as a hex integer. This ensures that repeated runs produce identical Rg trial statistics for the same ensemble, enabling reproducible benchmark tables without storing the random indices. The frame discovery logic searches subdirectories in priority order (`_relaxed`, `traj_pdbs`, `trajs`) with filename patterns (`frame_*.pdb`, `*_validated.pdb`, `*_relaxed.pdb`, `*_relax.pdb`, `*_raw.pdb`, `conformer_*.pdb`), matching the diverse output conventions of different ensemble generators.

Sources: [scoring/rg.py](/scoring/rg.py#L1-L135)

> [!TIP]
> When scoring large ensembles, chemical shift back-calculation dominates runtime. Ensure `CSPRED_PYTHON` and `CSPRED_PATH` are set correctly, and rely on the `cs_cache.csv` mechanism—once computed, shifts are restored from cache on subsequent runs without invoking CSpred.

> [!TIP]
> The `--normalize` flag does not re-score ensembles; it only aggregates existing `scores_trials.csv` files. Run the default scoring mode for each method/protein combination first, then invoke `--normalize` once with `--ens-base` pointing to the root of your multi-method directory hierarchy.

## Module Interaction Diagram

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Stack {
        +name: str
        +data: ndarray
        +sigma: dict|float
        +mu: dict|None
        +add(new_stack)
    }

    class XEISD {
        +exp_data: dict
        +bc_data: dict
        +pool_size: int
        +visited: dict
        +calc_scores(dtypes, indices) dict
        +optimize(opt_props, ens_size, beta) tuple
    }

    class BACK_Calculators {
        <<registry>>
        jc: jc_backcalc
        cs: cshift_backcalc
        noe: noe_backcalc
        pre: pre_backcalc
        fret: fret_backcalc
    }

    class ENSEMBLE_Scorers {
        <<registry>>
        jc: jc_score_ensemble
        cs: cs_score_ensemble
        noe: dist_score_ensemble
        pre: dist_score_ensemble
        fret: generic_score_ensemble
    }

    class EXP_DATA_LIB {
        <<lazy singleton>>
        protein → {dtype: filepath}
    }

    BACK_Calculators --> Stack : produces
    EXP_DATA_LIB --> XEISD : feeds
    Stack --> XEISD : initialized with
    ENSEMBLE_Scorers --> XEISD : dispatched by
    XEISD ..> Stack : reads bc_data
```

Sources: [scoring/parser.py](/scoring/parser.py#L24-L81), [scoring/calculator.py](/scoring/calculator.py#L243-L250), [scoring/scorer.py](/scoring/scorer.py#L127-L136), [scoring/optimizer.py](/scoring/optimizer.py#L21-L108)

## Data Flow: End-to-End Example

Consider scoring the α-synuclein (asyn) ensemble with PRE data. The CLI invocation `python score_ensemble.py asyn ./output/asyn --pre` triggers the following flow:

1. **Data resolution**: `EXP_DATA_LIB["asyn"]` lazily scans `Data/exp/asyn/` and discovers `asyn_pre_exp.txt` containing spin-label distance measurements with columns `index, res1, atom1, res2, atom2, dist_value, lower, upper`.
2. **Structure discovery**: PDBs are found via `glob("./output/asyn/*_relax*.pdb")`, invalid structures are pruned.
3. **Back-calculation**: `pre_backcalc` computes single-atom distances for each (res1, atom1)–(res2, atom2) pair across all conformers, substituting heavy atoms for hydrogens when needed (e.g., H → N for backbone amides).
4. **Stack construction**: `read_bc_data` wraps the distance matrix with σ_bc = 0.001 Å into a `Stack("pre", data, sigma=0.001)`.
5. **Trial scoring**: For each of 30 trials, 100 conformer indices are sampled; `dist_score_ensemble` computes the optimal correction parameters, evaluates the log-likelihood, and calculates MAE with asymmetric bounds.
6. **Output**: `scores_trials.csv` with columns `pre_mae, pre_score, rg`, plus console summary of mean ± stdev.

Sources: [score_ensemble.py](/score_ensemble.py#L44-L121), [scoring/calculator.py](/scoring/calculator.py#L155-L198), [data/asyn_pre_exp.txt](/data/asyn_pre_exp.txt#L1-L10)

## Integration with Downstream Pipelines

The X-EISD scoring module connects naturally with other IDPForge post-processing stages. Ensembles produced by [IDP Sampling](12-idp-sampling-fully-disordered) or [IDR Sampling](13-idr-sampling-with-folded-templates) should first undergo [AMBER Relaxation and Repair](15-amber-relaxation-and-repair) (producing `*_relax*.pdb` files) and optionally [Structure Validation](16-structure-validation-pipeline) (producing `*_validated.pdb` files) before scoring—back-calculation accuracy depends on physically realistic geometries. The `--normalize` workflow assumes a directory structure organized by generation method, enabling direct comparison of IDPForge ensembles against MD trajectories, FlexServ outputs, or other generators within the same benchmark framework.

# AlphaFlex Workflow Overview



The **AlphaFlex (AFX-IDPForge) pipeline** is a four-stage computational workflow that transforms AlphaFold2 predicted structures into physically realistic conformational ensembles for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Unlike the base IDPForge system—which operates on individual disordered segments in isolation—AlphaFlex orchestrates end-to-end processing: from IDR classification and database labeling, through per-region template construction and diffusion-based conformer generation, to Monte Carlo stitching of full-length multi-domain models with AMBER relaxation and structural validation. The pipeline is designed for high-throughput proteome-scale processing while remaining resumable and HPC-parallelizable at every stage.

Sources: [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L1-L146), [config.py](/AlphaFlex/config.py#L1-L123)

## Pipeline Architecture

The AlphaFlex pipeline processes proteins through four sequential stages, each consuming the outputs of the prior stage and writing results to a dedicated subdirectory under `Pipeline_Outputs/`. The central `config.py` module governs all tunable parameters and path defaults, ensuring consistent behavior across scripts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs
        DB[("AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json<br/>IDR boundaries + interactions")]
        LEN[("AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json<br/>Residue counts")]
        PDB[("AlphaFold2 PDB Library")]
        KNOT[("knot_screening.json<br/>Pre-computed topology")]
    end

    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Case Labeling"]
        S1[Step_1_case_label.py] -->|IDR type<br/>+ category| S1B[Step_1B_subset_label.py]
    end

    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Template Creation"]
        S2[Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py]
        S2 -->|Tail/Loop| MK_LDR[mk_ldr_template.py<br/>Static scaffold]
        S2 -->|Linker| MK_FLEX[mk_flex_template.py<br/>Dynamic scaffold]
        S2 -->|Category 0| IDP_JSON[idp_cases_to_run.json]
    end

    subgraph Step3["Step 3: Conformer Generation"]
        S3[Step_3_sample_conformer.py]
        S3 -->|IDR regions| SAMPLE_LDR[sample_ldr.py<br/>SE(3) diffusion]
        S3 -->|Full IDP| SAMPLE_IDP[sample_idp.py<br/>Unconditioned diffusion]
        S3 --> VALIDATE[Relax → Repair → Validate loop]
    end

    subgraph Step4["Step 4: Stitching & Minimization"]
        S4[Step_4_ldr_stitch.py]
        S4 -->|Single IDR| FASTPASS[Fast-Pass:<br/>Direct ensemble assembly]
        S4 -->|Multiple IDRs| MC[Monte Carlo Stitching:<br/>Kinematic chain assembly]
        MC --> RELAX[AMBER Relaxation<br/>+ Repair + Validation]
    end

    Inputs --> Step1
    Step1 -->|"labeled DB +<br/>subset .txt"| Step2
    PDB --> Step2
    Step2 -->|".npz templates"| Step3
    Step3 -->|"validated .pdb<br/>conformer pools"| Step4
    PDB --> Step4
    KNOT --> Step3
    KNOT --> Step4

    Step4 --> RESULT[("Final ensemble PDBs<br/>Category/Length/Protein/")]
```

Sources: [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L49-L141), [config.py](/AlphaFlex/config.py#L26-L123)

## IDR Classification System

The foundational abstraction of the AlphaFlex pipeline is its **four-tier IDR topology hierarchy**, which determines how each disordered region is processed downstream. The classification is hierarchical—higher categories imply greater structural complexity and require more sophisticated stitching strategies.

| Category | Name | Condition | Template Strategy | Stitching Complexity |
|:--------:|:----:|:----------|:------------------|:-------------------|
| **0** | IDP | Entire protein is disordered (no folded domains) | Unconditioned diffusion via `sample_idp.py` | Fast-pass (no stitching needed) |
| **1** | Tails | Only N/C-terminal IDRs; all internal regions are folded | Static scaffold via `mk_ldr_template.py` (frozen folded regions) | Low |
| **2** | Linkers | Internal IDRs between **non-interacting** folded domains | Dynamic scaffold via `mk_flex_template.py` (domains treated as separate rigid bodies with random displacements) | Medium (multi-body alignment) |
| **3** | Loops | Internal IDRs between **interacting** folded domains (mean PAE < 15 Å) | Static scaffold via `mk_ldr_template.py` (frozen folded regions) | High (constrained topology) |

Each IDR within a hybrid protein (Categories 1–3) receives a **disordered domain label** (`D1`, `D2`, …) and a **flanking domain annotation** identifying the adjacent folded domains (`F1`, `F2`, …). The interaction status between flanking domains—derived from the AlphaFold2 predicted aligned error (PAE) matrix—distinguishes Linkers from Loops and directly controls which template generation strategy is invoked.

Sources: [Step_1_case_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1_case_label.py#L1-L10), [Step_1_case_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1_case_label.py#L111-L197)

## Data Inputs and Resources

The pipeline depends on four pre-computed data resources stored in `AlphaFlex/Data_Inputs/`:

| File | Format | Content | Used By |
|------|--------|---------|---------|
| `AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json` | JSON dict | Per-protein IDR boundaries (`idrs`), mean inter-region PAEs (`mean_pae`), and folded domain interactions | Steps 1, 2, 4 |
| `AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json` | JSON dict | Total residue counts from AlphaFold2 9606 Human v4 | Steps 1, 1B |
| `knot_screening.json` | JSON dict | Per-domain knot presence/absence (`label`) and knot type (`closure_polys`) | Steps 3, 4 |
| `Test_Structures/O14653.pdb` | PDB | Sample Category 3 protein for pipeline testing | Steps 2, 3, 4 |

The master database is the central information artifact: each key is a UniProt accession, and values encode the spatial relationship between folded and disordered regions. Step 1 augments this database with computed labels, producing the **labeled database** that drives all downstream processing.

Sources: [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L7-L15), [config.py](/AlphaFlex/config.py#L18-L22)

## Step-by-Step Pipeline Walkthrough

### Step 1: Case Labeling → `Step_1_Labeling/`

This step reads the master database and classifies every protein into the four-tier category system. For each IDR, it computes: the residue **range**, the **type** (Tail/Linker/Loop/IDP), the ordinal **label** (D1, D2, …), and the **flanking domains**. The classification logic applies a strict hierarchy: if any Loop IDR is present, the protein is Category 3 regardless of other IDR types; Linkers take precedence over Tails; and a single IDR spanning the entire sequence yields Category 0.

The output is an augmented JSON database and an `idr_type_summary.txt` report showing the distribution across categories.

Sources: [Step_1_case_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1_case_label.py#L30-L199), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L49-L62)

### Step 1B: Subset Filtering → `Step_1_Labeling/custom_subsets/`

Step 1B creates filtered UniProt ID lists from the labeled database for targeted processing. It operates in two modes:

- **Basic mode** (length-only): Filters proteins by total residue count within `[min_len, max_len]`. All matching proteins are included regardless of IDR composition.
- **Advanced mode**: Additionally filters by per-type IDR counts (Tail/Linker/Loop) and a global IDR length range applied uniformly to every IDR in a protein. Count matching can be **exact** (default) or **minimum** (`--min_mode`).

Outputs include the filtered ID list (`.txt`), a per-protein report table, and—when advanced filters are active—an IDR length distribution histogram with bin counts.

Sources: [Step_1B_subset_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1B_subset_label.py#L1-L64), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L64-L80)

### Step 2: Template Creation → `Step_2_Templates/`

Step 2 generates per-IDR `.npz` structure templates for the diffusion model. For each protein in the subset ID list, it iterates over every labeled IDR and dispatches the appropriate template script based on IDR type:

- **Tail/Loop IDRs** → `mk_ldr_template.py`: Creates a **static scaffold** where all regions outside the specified IDR are held frozen. The disordered region is seeded with conformations distributed along the vector connecting its flanking folded domains.
- **Linker IDRs** → `mk_flex_template.py`: Creates a **dynamic scaffold** where the two adjacent folded domains are designated as separate rigid bodies and randomly displaced relative to one another, mimicking the flexibility of non-interacting domains.
- **Category 0 (Full IDP)** → No template is created; instead, the protein's sequence is logged to `idp_cases_to_run.json` for separate processing via `sample_idp.py` in Step 3.

An optional **truncation mode** (`--truncate`) builds each template on only the IDR plus its adjacent folded domains, reducing the template size for large proteins. Truncation sidecars (`.trunc.json`) record the offset and window boundaries for back-numbering during Step 4 reconstruction. A **graft-mode** alternative (`--max_residues`) caps template size while recording graft specifications for the `graft_back` utility.

Sources: [Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py#L1-L66), [Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py#L160-L286), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L82-L95)

### Step 3: Conformer Generation → `Step_3_Raw_Conformers/`

Step 3 generates validated conformer pools for each IDR template through an iterative **generate–relax–repair–validate** loop. Each IDR is processed independently, so proteins with multiple IDRs produce separate per-IDR conformer pools. The loop proceeds as follows:

1. **Generate + Relax**: Invokes `sample_ldr.py` (for IDR regions) or `sample_idp.py` (for full IDPs) to produce diffusion conformers, which are immediately relaxed via AMBER minimization using the configuration from `configs/sample.yml`.
2. **Repair**: Checks each relaxed structure for D-amino acids (chirality inversions) and broken histidine ring bonds. Applies fixes and re-relaxes if any repairs were made.
3. **Validate**: Runs unified validation checking chirality, bond integrity, clash score (using an **adaptive smart threshold**), and backbone topology (knot detection against the pre-computed `knot_screening.json`).

The loop continues until the target conformer count (`SAMPLE_N_CONFS`, default 10) is met or the maximum total attempts (`SAMPLE_MAX_TOTAL_ATTEMPTS`, default 500) is exhausted. **State persistence** via `.step3_state.json` enables recovery from cluster preemption—on restart, orphaned relaxed files from killed runs are automatically recovered. HPC parallel execution is supported through `--total_splits` and `--split_index` for deterministic sharding across jobs.

Sources: [Step_3_sample_conformer.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_3_sample_conformer.py#L1-L143), [Step_3_sample_conformer.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_3_sample_conformer.py#L178-L241), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L97-L113)

### Step 4: Stitching and Minimization → `Step_4_Final_Models/`

Step 4 assembles full-length protein models from the per-IDR conformer pools. Its behavior bifurcates based on IDR count:

**Single IDR / Full IDP (Fast-Pass):** Collects all validated conformers from Step 3 and combines them directly into a multi-model ensemble PDB. No stitching or additional minimization is performed.

**Multiple IDRs (Monte Carlo Stitching):** Runs a stochastic assembly loop that repeats until the target conformer count is reached or max attempts are exhausted. The kinematic chain assembly algorithm proceeds as:

1. Build a **segment map** partitioning the protein into alternating folded (F) and disordered (D) segments.
2. Seed the structure with the first folded domain from the AlphaFold2 prediction.
3. For each subsequent disordered segment, **draw a random conformer** from the per-IDR pool (round-robin with random shuffle).
4. **Superimpose** the middle 11 residues of the preceding folded domain (the "alignment stub") between the reference and conformer structures using Kabsch alignment.
5. **Overwrite** the reference structure with the aligned conformer coordinates from the stub onward. Repeat until all segments are stitched.
6. **Pre-relax repair**: flip any D-amino acids in the stitched structure.
7. **AMBER minimization** (ff14SB) with harmonic restraints on folded domains, allowing IDRs and junction regions to relax freely.
8. **Post-relax repair**: check for D-amino acids and broken HIS ring bonds introduced during relaxation; apply fixes and re-relax if needed.
9. **Validation**: chirality, bond integrity, clash score (adaptive smart threshold), backbone topology (knot detection), and **folded-domain curvature gate** (ensures relaxation did not distort well-structured regions beyond a configurable ratio).
10. Combine all valid conformers into a single multi-model ensemble PDB.

Final output is organized as `Step_4_Final_Models/<Category>/<Length_Label>/<protein_id>/<protein_id>_ensemble_n<N>.pdb`, where the length label stratifies proteins into bins (0–250, 251–500, 501–1000, etc.).

Sources: [Step_4_ldr_stitch.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_4_ldr_stitch.py#L1-L127), [Step_4_ldr_stitch.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_4_ldr_stitch.py#L218-L340), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L115-L141)

## Configuration Reference

All pipeline parameters are centralized in `config.py` and can be overridden via CLI arguments on each step script. The following table summarizes the key tunables organized by pipeline stage:

| Parameter | Default | Stage | Description |
|-----------|---------|:-----:|-------------|
| `VERBOSE` | `True` | All | Enable detailed per-protein console logging |
| `SUBSET_MIN_LENGTH` / `SUBSET_MAX_LENGTH` | 0 / 250 | 1B | Protein length range filter |
| `SUBSET_TAIL_COUNT` / `SUBSET_LINKER_COUNT` / `SUBSET_LOOP_COUNT` | 2 / 1 / 1 | 1B | Per-type IDR count constraints |
| `SUBSET_EXACT_COUNT` | `True` | 1B | Exact count matching vs. minimum |
| `SUBSET_IDR_MIN_LENGTH` / `SUBSET_IDR_MAX_LENGTH` | None | 1B | Global IDR length range (applied to all IDRs) |
| `TEMPLATE_N_CONFS` | 200 | 2 | Number of template conformations generated |
| `TEMPLATE_SEED_SKEW` | 0.5 | 2 | Seed distance skew for tail/loop templates on [d/2, d] |
| `TEMPLATE_FOLD_PER_SIDE` | 10 | 2 | Fold residues retained per junction in graft mode |
| `SAMPLE_N_CONFS` | 10 | 3 | Target validated conformers per IDR |
| `SAMPLE_BATCH_SIZE` | 6 | 3 | Diffusion batch size |
| `SAMPLE_MAX_TOTAL_ATTEMPTS` | 500 | 3 | Maximum generation attempts per IDR |
| `SAMPLE_FOLD_CURV_RATIO` | 0.5 | 3 | Folded-domain curvature gate ratio |
| `SAMPLE_JUNCTION_KAPPA` | 0.12 | 3 | Junction curvature gate (Å⁻¹) |
| `STITCH_N_CONFORMERS` | 10 | 4 | Target stitched conformers per protein |
| `STITCH_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | 500 | 4 | Maximum stitching attempts |
| `RELAX_STIFFNESS` | 10.0 | 4 | AMBER restraint strength on folded domains |
| `ALIGNMENT_STUB_HALF_SIZE` | 5 | 4 | Half-window for alignment stub (middle 11 residues) |
| `STITCH_BASE_CLASH_THRESHOLD` | 10.0 | 4 | Base clash score threshold (adaptive) |
| `STITCH_CLASH_INCREMENT` | 5.0 | 4 | Clash threshold escalation step per attempt tier |

Sources: [config.py](/AlphaFlex/config.py#L1-L123)

## Utility Modules

The `AlphaFlex/utils/` package provides shared functionality consumed primarily by Step 4:

| Module | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `stitch.py` | Kinematic chain assembly, segment mapping, BioPython superimposition, round-robin conformer drawing, ensemble directory discovery, PDB loading, length binning, and truncated-pool renumbering |
| `smart_scoring.py` | Adaptive clash threshold computation that escalates per-attempt tier, balancing validation strictness against throughput |
| `graft_back.py` | Graft-mode reconstruction: maps truncated sub-ensembles back to full-length numbering and grafts conformer coordinates onto the original AlphaFold2 scaffold |
| `truncate.py` | Computes IDR truncation windows (IDR + adjacent folded domains) for large-protein template size reduction |
| `file_ops.py` | Common file I/O helpers shared across pipeline steps |

The `assemble_kinematic_chain` function in `stitch.py` is the algorithmic core of Step 4: it partitions the protein into a segment map, then iteratively aligns and overwrites disordered conformers onto the growing model using the alignment stub superimposition strategy.

Sources: [stitch.py](/AlphaFlex/utils/stitch.py#L1-L23), [stitch.py](/AlphaFlex/utils/stitch.py#L291-L398)

## HPC and Resumability

The AlphaFlex pipeline is designed for proteome-scale throughput on HPC clusters. Key operational features include:

- **Deterministic sharding**: Steps 3 and 4 accept `--total_splits` and `--split_index` arguments that partition the protein ID list into non-overlapping chunks via `numpy.array_split`, enabling embarrassingly parallel job arrays.
- **State persistence**: Step 3 writes `.step3_state.json` after each generation round, recording the cumulative attempt count. On restart, the script detects existing validated files, recovers orphaned intermediate files, and resumes from the persisted state.
- **Progress tracking**: Step 2 writes `Step_2_progress.txt` recording the last processed protein ID, allowing batch resumption after interruption.
- **Per-protein logging**: Steps 3 and 4 stream per-protein logs to `logs/StepN/perprotein/split_K/<ID>.log`, enabling real-time monitoring via `tail -f` on long-running cluster jobs.
- **Local parallelism**: Step 4 additionally supports `--workers` for multi-process local parallel processing of stitching tasks.

Sources: [Step_3_sample_conformer.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_3_sample_conformer.py#L30-L56), [Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_2_mk_ldr_template.py#L111-L129), [README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L109-L141)

> [!TIP]
> The pipeline's iterative generate-relax-repair-validate loop in Step 3 is the primary throughput bottleneck. Tuning `SAMPLE_BATCH_SIZE` and `SAMPLE_MAX_TOTAL_ATTEMPTS` in `config.py` trades GPU utilization against conformer yield—larger batches amortize model loading overhead but increase per-round memory pressure. The adaptive clash threshold in Steps 3–4 automatically relaxes validation strictness as attempts mount, preventing infinite rejection loops on structurally challenging proteins.

> [!TIP]
> For proteins with multiple IDRs, the Monte Carlo stitching in Step 4 is stochastic by design—each run produces a different ensemble. The `ALIGNMENT_STUB_HALF_SIZE` parameter (default 5, yielding an 11-residue stub) controls the rigidity of the junction alignment: smaller stubs tolerate more local distortion at domain boundaries, while larger stubs enforce stricter continuity at the cost of reduced conformational diversity.

## Where to Go Next

The AlphaFlex workflow overview establishes the end-to-end processing narrative. To dive deeper into specific stages:

- **[Case Labeling and IDR Classification](19-case-labeling-and-idr-classification)** — Detailed mechanics of the four-tier category system, interaction-based Linker/Loop discrimination, and subset filtering strategies
- **[Monte Carlo Stitching and Assembly](20-monte-carlo-stitching-and-assembly)** — In-depth treatment of the kinematic chain algorithm, alignment stub superimposition, AMBER relaxation protocol, and adaptive validation gates
- **[IDR Sampling with Folded Templates](13-idr-sampling-with-folded-templates)** — How `sample_ldr.py` uses the `.npz` templates from Step 2 to condition SE(3) backbone diffusion on folded-domain context
- **[AMBER Relaxation and Repair](15-amber-relaxation-and-repair)** — The ff14SB minimization protocol, chirality repair, and histidine ring bond correction used in Steps 3 and 4
- **[Structure Validation Pipeline](16-structure-validation-pipeline)** — Unified validation checks including adaptive clash scoring, knot detection, and folded-domain curvature gating

# Case Labeling and IDR Classification



The AlphaFlex pipeline's entry point is a **topological classification system** that categorizes every human protein into one of four hierarchical categories based on the spatial arrangement and interaction context of its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This classification, implemented in `Step_1_case_label.py`, transforms raw AlphaFold2-derived annotation data into a labeled database that drives all downstream template generation, conformer sampling, and stitching decisions. The subsequent `Step_1B_subset_label.py` then provides powerful filtering capabilities to carve out targeted protein subsets for batch processing. Together, these two scripts form the classification and selection gateway of the entire AFX-IDPForge pipeline.

Sources: [Step_1_case_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1_case_label.py#L1-L10), [Step_1B_subset_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1B_subset_label.py#L1-L7)

## The Four-Category Taxonomy

The classification system assigns each protein to exactly one category based on a **priority hierarchy** that reflects increasing structural complexity. A protein containing any Loop IDR is automatically Category 3, even if it also contains Tails or Linkers—this is by design, because Loop IDRs between interacting domains impose the strictest geometric constraints during conformer assembly and require the most sophisticated stitching strategies.

| Category | Name | Definition | IDR Topology | Downstream Template Strategy |
|----------|------|------------|--------------|------------------------------|
| **0** | **IDP** | Fully disordered—no folded domains exist | Single IDR spanning residues 1 → N | Full diffusion via `sample_idp.py` (no folded scaffold) |
| **1** | **Tails** | Folded domain(s) with only terminal IDRs | One or both termini are disordered; no internal IDRs | Static template via `mk_ldr_template.py` (frozen folded core) |
| **2** | **Linkers** | Internal IDRs between non-interacting folded domains | At least one internal IDR where flanking F-domains are non-interacting (PAE ≥ 15Å) | Flexible template via `mk_flex_template.py` (mobile domain objects) |
| **3** | **Loops** | Internal IDRs between interacting folded domains | At least one internal IDR where flanking F-domains interact (PAE < 15Å) | Static template via `mk_ldr_template.py` (interacting domains held rigid) |

The critical distinction between Category 2 (Linkers) and Category 3 (Loops) lies in whether the folded domains flanking an internal IDR **interact**. This is determined from the `interactions` field in the master database, which records pairs of folded domains whose mean Predicted Aligned Error (PAE) falls below 15 Ångströms—indicating they form a stable structural unit. When flanking domains interact, the IDR forms a **Loop** that bridges a compact structural unit and must be modeled with both domains held rigid. When they do not interact, the IDR forms a **Linker** connecting independently mobile domains that can be repositioned during template generation.

Sources: [Step_1_case_label.py](/AlphaFlex/Step_1_case_label.py#L4-L9), [AlphaFlex/README.md](/AlphaFlex/README.md#L49-L62)

## Input Data Architecture

The classification engine consumes two pre-built JSON databases derived from the AlphaFold2 9606 Human v4 predictions:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph MasterDB["AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json"]
        direction TB
        IDR["idrs: IDR boundary pairs<br/>e.g. [[1,21], [147,181]]"]
        PAE["mean_pae: Inter-region PAE map<br/>e.g. F1-F2: 2.99"]
        INT["interactions: Interacting F-domain pairs<br/>e.g. [[F1,F2]]"]
    end

    subgraph LengthRef["AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json"]
        direction TB
        LEN["Total residue count<br/>e.g. A0A075B6H9: 96"]
    end

    MasterDB --> Classifier["Step 1<br/>Case Labeling"]
    LengthRef --> Classifier
    Classifier --> LabeledDB["Labeled Database<br/>(augmented master DB)"]
    Classifier --> Summary["idr_type_summary.txt<br/>(category distribution)"]
```

The **master database** (`AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json`) is keyed by UniProt accession and contains three fields per protein: `idrs` (an ordered list of `[start, end]` residue pairs defining each disordered segment), `mean_pae` (a dictionary of mean PAE values between all region pairs—folded and disordered), and `interactions` (a list of folded domain pairs where the inter-domain PAE is below 15 Å, signaling structural interaction). The **length reference** (`AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json`) maps each UniProt ID to its total residue count, which is essential for detecting N/C-terminal IDRs and full-IDP cases.

> [!TIP]
> The `interactions` field is the sole determinant of the Linker vs. Loop distinction. If `interactions` is empty or does not contain a given F-domain pair, the IDR between them is classified as a Linker. This binary decision has significant downstream consequences: Linkers receive flexible templates with randomly repositioned folded domains, while Loops are constrained to a static scaffold.

Sources: [AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json](/AlphaFlex/Data_Inputs/AlphaFlex_database_Nov2025.json#L1-L55), [AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json](/AlphaFlex/Data_Inputs/AF2_9606_HUMAN_v4_num_residues.json#L1-L12)

## Classification Algorithm in Detail

The classification proceeds through a single pass over all proteins in the master database. For each protein, the algorithm follows a three-stage decision process:

**Stage 1 — Full IDP Detection (Category 0):** If the protein has exactly one IDR and that IDR spans from residue 1 to the total protein length, the entire chain is disordered. This is the simplest case: the IDR is labeled as type `"IDP"` with label `"D1"` and no flanking domains.
